62630.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse trylla (“to enchant; turn into a troll”), from Proto-Germanic *truzlijaną (“to perform magic, conjure”), a causative or denominative derivative of *truzlą (“troll, supernatural being”). The original sense was “to turn someone into a troll”, hence more generally “to transform or bewitch through magic”. The intransitive sense “to practise magic” and the modern sense “to perform conjuring tricks as entertainment” developed from this.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk trylle and trylla, Danish trylle, Swedish trylla, Icelandic trylla, and Middle High German Middle High German trül

Variant of Anna, first attested in the 15th century. The name ultimately derives from Latin Anna, from Ancient Greek Ἄννα (Ánna), from Biblical Hebrew חַנָּה (Ḥannāh, “grace, favour”), from חָנַן (ḥānan, “to be gracious, show favour”). Doublet of Hannah (“female given name”).
The Biblical Hebrew name חַנָּה (Ḥannāh) is borne in the Hebrew Bible by Hannah, the mother of Samuel. Its Greek form Ἄννα (Ánna) occurs in the New Testament as the name of Anna the Prophetess.
